boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's battle of Austerlitz (2 December 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the allied attack on the French right at Telnitz and Sokolnitz, the French attack on the Pratzen heights that broke the allied centre, Bagration's and Liechtenstein's fight against the French left, and the allied retreat that night to Hodiegitz. The allied advance from Olmütz from 27 November is context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) under Napoleon I 97 battalions and 50,000 infantry, 121 squadrons and 15,000 cavalry and 282 guns, a total strength of 65,000, and side B (Russians and Austrians) under General Kutusow 114 battalions and 67,000 infantry, 148 squadrons and 16,000 cavalry and 300 guns, a total strength of 83,000, of which, by his footnote, 21 battalions and 28 squadrons, 16,000 men, were Austrians. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the battle, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed table, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. For side B, Schönhals's order of battle of the allied army at Austerlitz sums to 114 battalions, 10 companies, 170¾ squadrons, 82575 men and 16565 horses (claim schoenhals-side-b): Bodart's 114 battalions are the table's, his 83,000 is its 82575 rounded up to the thousand, and 82575 less the 16565 horses leaves 66010, which rounded up is his 67,000 infantry (our arithmetic); but his 148 squadrons and 16,000 cavalry are not the table's 170¾ squadrons and 16565 horses, the table gives no guns, and the passages read do not show how he reckoned. Victoires et conquêtes gives an effective of eighty-two thousand and forty men, about eighteen thousand of them Austrians, on the march of 27 November, and nearly a hundred thousand allies against sixty to seventy thousand French in line (claim victoires-side-b). For side A, his 65,000 is the strength the French themselves give, by Schönhals's account, and Dumas's figure for the whole French army as Schönhals reports it (claim schoenhals-side-a), and lies within Victoires's sixty to seventy thousand French troops in line (claim victoires-side-a); his battalions, squadrons and guns for side A are in none of the passages read. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the table: '1805 2/12. battle at Austerlitz (1.)'; 'French | Russians and Austrians'; 'Napoleon I | Gen. Kutusow'; '97 battalions 50,000 | infantry | 67,000 battalions 114'; '121 squadrons 15,000 | cavalry | 16,000 squadrons 148'; '282 guns 65,000 | total strength | 83,000 [1] guns 300'; '[1] of which 21 battalions, 28 squadrons = 16,000 Austrians'.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account in Victoires et conquêtes: the total force of the French troops in line hardly rose above sixty to seventy thousand men, against nearly a hundred thousand allies. Napoleon had sent orderly officers in all haste to bring the corps of Bernadotte and Davoust up into line (OCR). On the eve of the battle it places Lannes's divisions Suchet and Caffarelli on the left, Bernadotte's corps, then only the divisions Rivaud and Drouet, in the centre behind the village of Jirzokowith, Murat's cavalry corps to the left of and a little behind Bernadotte, Soult's divisions Legrand, Vandamme and Saint-Hilaire on the right, and near Turas a reserve of ten battalions of the imperial guard and ten battalions of Oudinot's grenadiers with forty guns in the intervals. Of Davoust's corps, Friant's division and a dragoon division were sent to the convent of Reygern, and Gudin's division was to come from Nikolsburg to contain Meerveldt (OCR). Twenty thousand of the army's soldiers did not burn a cartridge; the reserve did not fire a shot during the battle, and the guard on foot and Oudinot's grenadiers asked in vain to be engaged (OCR).
claims.rationale: Side A's compilation, read from the page images (pp. 238-239 and 267) except the call to Bernadotte and Davoust (p. 230), the beginning of the sentence on Bernadotte's corps and the detachments to Reygern and against Meerveldt (p. 237) and the reserve's idleness (pp. 247 and 270), all OCR. The sixty to seventy thousand are the troops in line; Victoires gives no figure for the whole army, and the passages read do not say whether the detachments are counted in them. Napoleon called up and placed his corps, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'the total force of the French troops in line hardly rose beyond sixty to seventy thousand men; the allies had nearly a hundred thousand' (p. 239); 'meanwhile the corps of Marshals Bernadotte and Davoust, to which the Emperor Napoleon had sent orderly officers in all haste, were advancing to come into line' (p. 230, OCR); 'the divisions Suchet and Caffarelli, of Marshal Lannes's corps, formed the left of the army and touched Murat's cavalry'; 'the corps of Marshal Bernadotte, forming the centre and composed on-' (p. 237, OCR) '-ly then of the divisions Rivaud and Drouet, was placed behind the village of Jirzokowith, which was itself strongly occupied' (p. 238); 'Murat's cavalry corps was to the left of and a little behind Bernadotte's troops'; 'Marshal Soult commanded the right wing, composed of the division Legrand, which formed its extremity and was in position between the villages of Sokolnitz and Telnitz; of the division Vandamme, which held the left, and of the division Saint-Hilaire, forming the centre and placed to the left of Kobelnitz'; 'the army's reserve, composed of ten battalions of the imperial guard and ten battalions of General Oudinot's grenadiers, was near Turas, between that village and Schlapanitz'; 'this reserve was drawn up in two lines, in columns, by battalion at deploying distance, having in the intervals forty pieces of' (p. 238) 'cannon. It was with it that Napoleon planned to throw himself wherever he believed his presence urgent' (p. 239); 'the Emperor had a division of this corps (that of General Friant) and another of dragoons sent to the convent of Reygern, to observe and contain the enemy's left there, in case it advanced by the Auspitz road' (p. 237, OCR); 'the division Gudin was to move from Nikolsburg, where it had arrived coming from Presburg, onto the right of the French line, to contain General Meerveldt' (p. 237, OCR); 'the loss of the French army, of which twenty thousand soldiers had not burnt a cartridge' (p. 267), as in claim side-a-losses-reported; 'this reserve did not fire a musket shot during the battle' (p. 247, OCR); 'in the course of the day the imperial guard on foot and Oudinot's grenadiers showed their impatience at not being engaged with the enemy, and asked to be sent in: "Rejoice at doing nothing", the emperor answered, "I am keeping you in reserve; so much the better if you are not needed today."' (p. 270, OCR).

claims.value: Side A (French) in Schönhals, the Austrian account: the strength of the French is not known; they themselves give it as 65.000 men, and Dumas gives the whole French army as 65.000 combatants. It is thought, Schönhals says, that the allies were somewhat stronger than the French, but the superiority cannot have been significant. Neither the French Guard infantry nor Oudinot's grenadier division had been in action. Behind Schlappanitz the Guards under Bessières and grenadier battalions under Oudinot, with guns, stood in reserve under Marshal Duroc, and Davoust with Friant's division and the dragoons under 'Pourcier' (so the OCR) was detached to observe the convent of Raigern, with Gudin's division toward Nikolsburg to hold Merveldt's corps in check (OCR). At the Kobelnitz pond a brigade of Oudinot's division stood in the way of beaten allied columns (OCR).
claims.rationale: Side B's history on side A, read from the page images (pp. 156 and 169) except the reserve and the detachments (p. 158) and the brigade at the Kobelnitz pond (p. 167), OCR. By its preface Schönhals draws what it says of the French army's operations from that army's bulletins, and here it cites Dumas. Its p. 169 says neither the Guard infantry nor Oudinot's grenadier division had been in action, while its p. 167 (OCR) has a brigade of Oudinot's division bar the way of beaten columns at the Kobelnitz pond; the passages read do not reconcile the two. The reserve and the detachments were Napoleon's dispositions, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'the strength of the French is not known; they themselves give it as 65.000 men'; 'it is, however, the opinion that the allies were somewhat stronger than the French'; 'in no case, however, could this superiority be significant' (p. 156); 'Dumas says 800 dead, 6000 wounded, in which he gives the whole strength of the French army as 65.000 combatants'; 'neither the French Guard infantry nor the grenadier division Oudinot had been in action' (p. 169); 'north-west on the height behind Schlappanitz stood as reserve the Guards under Bessières, ... (OCR) grenadier battalions under Oudinot with ... (OCR) guns, the whole commanded by Marshal Duroc' (p. 158, OCR); 'to observe the point of the convent of Raigern on the Schwarzawa, Davoust with the division Friant and the dragoons under Pourcier, and toward Nikolsburg the division Gudin, were detached, to hold Merveldt's corps in check' (p. 158, OCR); 'the remnants of the ... (OCR) and almost the whole ... (OCR) were pressed against the Kobelnitz pond and tried to save themselves over its ice cover, but here a brigade of Oudinot's division stood in their way' (p. 167, OCR).

claims.value: Side B in Victoires et conquêtes: the Grand Duke Constantine arrived at Olmutz on 25 November with nine thousand men of the Russian imperial guard, which brought the combined army to more than eighty thousand men, and another reinforcement of ten thousand men under General Essen was only a few marches away. On the march of 27 November it gives the guard, the reserve under Constantine, as ten battalions, eighteen squadrons and four companies of artillery, eight thousand five hundred men in all, and all the columns, with the advance guard, the Russian reserve and Kienmayer's cavalry reserve, as an effective of eighty-two thousand and forty men, about eighteen thousand of them Austrians. For the eve of the battle it gives the allies nearly a hundred thousand, and Napoleon's proclamation of 3 December speaks of an army of a hundred thousand men. The centre, Kollowrath's column, was made up of rather weak battalions, its Russian regiments those that had retreated from Braunau and fought at Diernstein, and its Austrian battalions nearly all new levies (OCR).
claims.rationale: Side A's compilation on side B, read from the page images (pp. 226-227, 239 and 268) except Kollowrath's column (p. 249, OCR). Victoires's figures differ among themselves: nine thousand (p. 226) and eight thousand five hundred (p. 227) for the guard; more than eighty thousand on 25 November and eighty-two thousand and forty on the march of the 27th, against nearly a hundred thousand on p. 239 and the hundred thousand of Napoleon's proclamation, an address to his army, not a return. Its about eighteen thousand Austrians compare with Bodart's 16,000 (claim bodart-strength). In Schönhals, Essen was still awaited and stood at Kremsier on the day of the battle without taking part (claim decision-to-attack, OCR). The army was the force the allied sovereigns had assembled under Kutusow, so for the battle the claim is tagged inherited. claims.value: Bodart places side A (French) under Napoleon I in the left column of his table, the winner's place by his stated rule, so he records a victory of side A over side B (Russians and Austrians) under General Kutusow on 2 December. In Victoires, General Dochtorow, protected by the cavalry, almost all Austrian, halted on the heights of Neudorf and tried to restore order among his battalions, still a mass of eight thousand men, and night alone saved these remnants of the allied left from the French pursuit; the Austrian cavalry formed the rearguard, unpursued by the French, who stayed on their side of the dike; the allies retreated through the night by Boschowitz, the two emperors withdrew behind Austerlitz to the position of Hodiegitz, and the victorious army crowned the position the beaten army had held the night before. In Schönhals, the French army stayed after its victory in the position the allied army had held the day before, the allied army withdrew in the night behind Austerlitz to the position of Hodiegitz, and the column of the allied left, still about 8000 men, gathered again only at Neudorf.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's table and rule, with the other accounts' ending, read from the page images. No source read gives a different result; both other accounts have the French army hold the ground the allies had held the day before and the allies retreat in the night behind Austerlitz to Hodiegitz, and both have the beaten column of the allied left gather again at Neudorf, eight thousand men in Victoires and about 8000 in Schönhals. English renderings (ours): Bodart, p. 46, 'the winner's place in the comparisons is always to be sought on the left side, the loser's on the right'; the table as in claim bodart-strength; Victoires, 'General Dochtorow, thus protected by the devotion of the cavalry, almost all Austrian, halted on the heights of Neudorf, where he strove to restore order in his battalions, which still formed a mass of eight thousand men'; 'it was half past four in the evening, and the night, which was beginning to spread its veils, alone could save these remnants of the enemy's left from the ardent pursuit of the French'; 'the Austrian cavalry formed the rearguard, without being followed by the French, who stayed on this side of the dike'; 'the retreat continued by Boschowitz: the Austro-Russians marched all night through an abundant and icy rain, which finished ruining the roads and bogging down what remained of the artillery'; 'the two emperors of Austria and Russia, after taking great pains to gather all that had escaped from the battlefield, withdrew behind Austerlitz into the position of Hodiegitz'; 'the victorious army crowned the position that the beaten army had occupied the night before' (p. 266); Schönhals, 'the French army stayed, after the victory won, in the position that the allied army had held the day before; the latter withdrew that same night behind Austerlitz into the position of Hodiegitz'; 'the column, still consisting of about 8000 men, gathered again only at Neudorf and continued its retreat toward Boschowitz, before which place it bivouacked' (p. 169).

claims.value: Bodart gives side A's (French) loss as 10,000 killed and wounded (14 generals, 80 staff officers and 514 officers), 15·3 per cent, with no prisoners, 10,000 in all (608 officers), and 1 eagle lost; and side B's (Russian and Austrian) as 16,000 killed and wounded (9 generals and 293 officers), 19·3 per cent, and 20,000 prisoners (9 generals and 820 officers), 24·1 per cent, 36,000 in all (1,131 officers), 43·4 per cent, of which, by his footnote, the Austrian loss was 6,000 men, 38 per cent, with 186 guns (62 per cent), 45 flags and 400 ammunition wagons lost. He records the French Brigadier-General Valhubert, the Russian Lieutenant-General Count Essen and the Austrian GM von Juerczik as killed.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed losses, rounded up by his rule (claim bodart-strength); a post-outcome observation. His percentages are of each side's strength: 16,000, 20,000 and 36,000 of 83,000 are 19.3, 24.1 and 43.4 per cent, 186 of 300 guns 62 per cent, and 6,000 of the 16,000 Austrians 37.5 per cent, printed 38, while 10,000 of 65,000 is 15.38 per cent, printed 15·3 (our arithmetic). The 608 officers are 14 + 80 + 514, and the 1,131 are 9 + 293 + 9 + 820, generals included (our arithmetic). Schönhals's 5922 Austrian dead, wounded and prisoners round up to his 6,000 (our arithmetic; claim side-b-losses-reported); his other losses are in none of the passages read, and his 45 flags equal Victoires's forty-five (claim side-a-losses-reported). His officer-loss table for the battle is not in the frame transcription. Of his fallen generals, Victoires has Valhubert die of his wounds (claim side-a-losses-reported); the passages read do not report Count Essen's or Juerczik's death. Victoires names a lieutenant-general Essen among the generals under Liechtenstein on the march of 27 November, and Schönhals has a GL Essen with a corps at Kremsier on the day of the battle (OCR); the passages read do not show whether either is Bodart's Count Essen. claims.value: Side B's loss in the other accounts. Victoires: the allies had more than forty thousand men out of action; eighteen thousand Russians and six hundred Austrians were killed by fire or drowned, the rest wounded or taken, among the prisoners fifteen generals and more than four hundred Russian officers of all ranks; the Russians lost forty-five flags and almost all the standards of their imperial guard. Napoleon's proclamation of 3 December claims forty flags, the standards of the Russian imperial guard, a hundred and twenty guns, twenty generals and more than thirty thousand prisoners, and says that what escaped the French fire drowned in the two lakes. Victoires's narrative has Przybyszewsky taken prisoner in the valley of Sokolnitz and the columns there lose all their artillery, a very great number of officers and soldiers drown where the ice of the pond broke, and an artillery park with its escort swallowed when the ice of the Augezd lake broke under it (OCR). Schönhals: only the Austrian corps' loss can be given exactly, 5922 dead, wounded and prisoners; the Russian army may have lost about 15.000 prisoners and 5000 to 6000 dead and wounded; the drowning of so many Russians in the ponds belongs among the French exaggerations, for though the ice broke here and there under the fugitives, the ponds were on the whole frozen very hard and the Russians drowned were certainly very few, and it cites the Tellnitz parish priest for their number (OCR). The remaining guns had to be left stuck in the muddy road; only Kienmayer's corps saved its guns.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images (Victoires pp. 266-268 and 271; Schönhals p. 169) except Victoires's sentences on Sokolnitz, the ice and the gun park (pp. 262 and 264) and Schönhals's sentence on the Tellnitz priest (p. 170), OCR; not combined. Schönhals's Russian figures make 20,000 to 21,000 and, with the Austrians, 25,922 to 26,922 (our arithmetic), against Victoires's more than forty thousand and Bodart's 36,000, of which 6,000 Austrians (claim bodart-losses). Victoires's six hundred Austrians are its Austrians killed or drowned, not their whole loss. The prisoners differ: fifteen generals among them in Victoires's narrative, twenty generals and more than thirty thousand prisoners in the proclamation, an address to the army, not a return, about 15.000 Russians in Schönhals, and 20,000 with 9 generals in Bodart; the flags differ too, forty-five in Victoires's narrative and in Bodart, forty in the proclamation. The two accounts dispute the drowning, and Schönhals's own p. 169 grants that the enemy's fire broke openings in the ice in which a number of fugitives perished, few on the whole. English renderings (ours): Victoires, 'the allies had more than forty thousand men out of' (p. 266) 'action in this memorable day, to which Napoleon gave the name of battle of Austerlitz; eighteen thousand Russians and six hundred Austrians were killed by fire or drowned, the rest wounded or taken prisoner, and among the latter fifteen generals and more than four hundred Russian officers of all ranks' (p. 267); as in claim side-a-losses-reported for the flags; 'forty flags, the standards of the imperial guard of Russia, a hundred and twenty pieces of cannon, twenty generals, more than thirty thousand prisoners are the result of this day for ever famous' (p. 268); as in claim victoires-side-b for the proclamation, its hundred thousand and the lakes; 'Lieutenant-General Przybyschevvsky and ... (OCR) men were taken prisoner in the valley of Sokolnitz; there was about an equal number killed and drowned, and both columns lost all their artillery' (p. 262, OCR); 'some battalions succeeded in crossing the pond; but the ice, giving way under the weight of the others, broke, and a very great number of officers and soldiers drowned there' (p. 262, OCR); 'a park of ... (OCR) pieces of artillery, marching under the guard of ... (OCR) battalions, tried to follow an old submerged dike, formerly a communication across the lake of Augezd between the village of that name and that of Satschau; but the ice that covered the lake, not being strong enough to bear this enormous weight, broke when the convoy was in the middle of the lake: men, horses, guns, caissons, all was swallowed' (p. 264, OCR); Schönhals, 'of the loss on both sides only that of the Austrian corps can be given with exactness; it amounted in dead, wounded and prisoners to 5922 men'; 'the Russian army may well have lost about 15.000 prisoners and 5000 to 6000 dead and wounded'; 'the drowning of so many Russians in the ponds belongs among the French exaggerations'; 'the ice did break here and there under the weight of the fugitives, but on the whole the ponds were frozen very hard, and the number of drowned Russians was certainly very insignificant;' (p. 169); '[by the state]ment of the Tellnitz parish priest they may be put at ... (OCR) to at most ... claims.value: Bodart describes Austerlitz as a town in Moravia, 20 km east of Brünn. Schönhals describes the field (OCR): a small brook flows south from the wooded heights past Bellowitz and Schlappanitz, forming marshy meadows and a defile hard for columns to cross; below it the large ponds of Satczan and Mönitz continue the defile, which is hard to pass at Tellnitz and Sokolnitz, villages surrounded by fences and ditches; between this defile and the Schwarzawa the land is almost wholly level between Turas and Latein and allows every arm free use; north of the road a steep hill with a chapel on its top commands the Olmütz road and the approach to the Bellowitz defile; and from Augezd a ridge runs north toward Pratze, on which the allied army was camped, a strong position that allowed an emphatic use of artillery against an attack. Victoires calls the santon, the height on which Lannes's left rested, a very favourable position. Both accounts make the Pratzen height the key: lying at the centre of the position, its holding by the French cut off the allied left (Schönhals, OCR), and its occupation decided the battle (Victoires, OCR). A thick fog lay over the ground and hid Napoleon's position from the allies (Schönhals, OCR), and the fog in the valley and the smoke of the bivouacs hid the French advance on Pratzen (Victoires, OCR). claims.value: The allied aim was to turn the French right and cut the French army off from Vienna. Schönhals: the plan of operations approved by both monarchs was at the outset to make the enemy retreat behind the Thaya by gaining his right flank and threatening his communication with Vienna, and, if he ignored the threat, to attack his right flank decisively, throw him back on the Znaim road and force his retreat toward Krems, with Archduke Ferdinand's corps from Iglau to take part (OCR); the disposition for the battle had the allied left, which overlapped the French right, force the defiles of Sokolnitz and Tellnitz and continue the attack on open ground between Schlappanitz and Turas, avoiding the Schlappanitz and Bellowitz defile; the attack was to be in oblique order, Bagration's corps on the extreme right to hold its position for the time being and Liechtenstein's cavalry in the centre to cover the open ground between Kruch and Schlappanitz. Victoires: Kutusow's plan was to attack Napoleon's army by its right flank with great masses, the valley between Telnitz and Sokolnitz to be crossed at the run under cover of Liechtenstein's cavalry and Bagration's advance guard on the allied right; he wanted to cut the French army's retreat on Vienna (OCR) and to turn it and force it to lay down its arms (OCR). Victoires calls the plan vicious even on the Russian general's own suppositions (OCR).
claims.rationale: Aims of side B's command as both accounts give them, from the page images (Victoires p. 239; Schönhals p. 156) and the OCR (Victoires pp. 230 and 240; Schönhals p. 150). The accounts agree on the plan of the battle: to turn the French right through the defiles of Sokolnitz and Telnitz and continue the attack in the plain toward Turas, avoiding the Schlappanitz and Bellowitz defile, with Bagration and Liechtenstein covering on the right. The aims were the allied commanders' choices, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Schönhals, 'the plan of future operations approved by both monarchs had as its aim, with the forces always to be kept together, to try at the outset to bring the enemy to retreat behind the Thaya by gaining his right flank and threatening his communication with Vienna' (p. 150, OCR); 'in case the enemy did not heed this strategic threat, a decisive attack against his right flank was intended, to throw him back on the Znaim road and force him to retreat toward Krems, in which the corps of Archduke Ferdinand, approaching from Iglau, was also to take part' (p. 150, OCR); 'accordingly the left wing of the allies considerably overlapped the right of the French'; 'the attack on the latter was held to be subject to the fewest difficulties, because it was believed that after forcing the defiles of Sokolnitz and Tellnitz one would stand wholly on its flank and could continue the further attack on the open ground between Schlappanitz and Turas'; 'by this movement one wanted to avoid entirely the defile of Schlappanitz and Bellowitz, by which (so it was imagined) the enemy had been at pains to cover his front'; 'everything would depend on this plan being carried out in time and with the greatest possible force'; 'the attack was thus to take place in oblique order, and the corps of Prince Bagration, which formed the extreme right wing, was for the moment merely to hold its position, and Prince Liechtenstein's cavalry in the centre was to endeavour to cover the open ground between Kruch and Schlappanitz to the left and right of the road' (p. 156); Victoires, 'the left of the combined army overlapped the right of the French army'; 'Kutusow supposed that in passing the defile of Sokolnitz and Kobelnitz the right of the French would find itself turned, and that the attack could then be continued in the plain between Schlapanitz and the wood of Turas, thus avoiding the defiles of Schlapanitz and Bellovitz, which, in the Russian general's opinion, covered the front of the French position'; 'so his plan was to attack Napoleon's army by its right flank, on which great masses were to move with speed and vigour'; 'the valley between Telnitz and Sokolnitz was to be crossed at the run; the cavalry of Prince Lichstenstein and the advance guard of Prince Bagration, forming the right of the allied army, were to cover this movement:' (p. 239); 'he wanted to cut off the French army's retreat on Vienna' (p. 230, OCR); 'in this belief General Kutusow, instead of hastening his frontal movement, resolved to manoeuvre so as to turn the French army and force it to lay down its arms' (p. 230, OCR); 'this plan was vicious, even on the Russian general's suppositions:' (p. 240, OCR).

claims.value: Side A fortified the santon, a position from which it fought: Napoleon had the height on which Lannes's left rested fortified and occupied with all the more care because he regarded it as the key of his offensive operations; eighteen guns were placed there in battery, and the seventeenth light infantry regiment under General Claparède of Suchet's division held it. Bagration attacked it without yet knowing its strength, and the French artillery soon forced the Russians back to Posorzitz (Victoires, OCR); in Schönhals, Bagration's general advance brought on a murderous cannonade, which the enemy kept up with the greater success from his commanding position because the Russian batteries stood lower (OCR). Schönhals has the village in front of Lannes's wing occupied with guns and a light infantry regiment under Claparède (OCR) and does not call it fortified. Before the battle Napoleon had retrenchments built with much show and garnished with artillery on the heights his advance guard then crowned, as if he meant to keep them (Victoires, OCR); in its account he later withdrew his outposts to Telnitz, Sokolnitz and Schlapanitz (OCR), and the passages read do not say that those works were used in the battle. The retrenchments built for show before the battle and the ditch at Telnitz are recorded but do not decide the code: the former stood on heights the French then gave up, by Victoires's account, and the latter is a ditch of the village, which Victoires calls a natural retrenchment. open_questions: Deferred: the bulletins of the Grande Armée and Napoleon's correspondence, the corps reports from which Victoires says the French loss was estimated, and Savary's account, none inspected; Russian accounts of the battle, which neither account cites in the passages read; Dumas's Précis, which Schönhals cites for the French strength and loss, not inspected; the enclosure (Beilage) that Schönhals's p. 156 says gives the strength of the Austrian troops and of Merveldt's corps, not inspected; Alombert and Colin's t. IV, which ends before Ober-Hollabrunn and so before this battle; Bodart's officer-loss table for the battle, not in the frame transcription; the body of Schönhals's order of battle (pp. 177-178), transcribed only for the 3rd column and the recapitulation, the battalion sums of its other blocks having been checked on the images against the recapitulation; Victoires's footnote (OCR) in which a captured Langeron names the Emperor Alexander and then Kutusow as commanding the Russian army, read and not cited; and the narratives of the fighting in the north (Liechtenstein, Constantine, Murat and Bernadotte) in both accounts, read and cited only where they bear on the dimensions. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: Kollowrath's column, the fighting at Telnitz and Sokolnitz, the prisoners and guns taken at Sokolnitz, at Augezd and in the night, the gun park on the Augezd lake, the Austrian loss on the Pratzen heights, Bagration's loss, Przybyszewsky's capture, the drowned by the Tellnitz priest's count, the French reserve's guns, the allied consumers, Essen's and Archduke Charles's strengths, the hours of the allied march and of Napoleon's order to attack; the page numbers of the OCR quotes, read from the OCR running heads and page breaks.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength. Bodart gives 83,000 (67,000 infantry and 16,000 cavalry in 114 battalions and 148 squadrons, 16,000 of them Austrians); Victoires gives eighty-two thousand and forty on the march of 27 November and nearly a hundred thousand on the eve of the battle; Schönhals nearly 89.000 men and 20.000 horses on 25 November. The targeted follow-up registered and read Schönhals's order of battle of the allied army at Austerlitz (pp. 177-178, page images; claim schoenhals-side-b): its recapitulation sums to 114 battalions, 10 companies, 170¾ squadrons, 82575 men and 16565 horses, so Bodart's 114 battalions and 83,000 agree with it (82575 rounded up, our arithmetic), while his 148 squadrons and 16,000 cavalry are not the table's 170¾ squadrons and 16565 horses; the table gives no guns, three companies and a squadron of horse artillery arrived only after the battle, and the 3rd column's rows sum to 16 battalions against the recapitulation's 18. The table does not separate the Austrians, so Bodart's 16,000 Austrians and Victoires's about eighteen thousand remain unchecked; the enclosure on the Austrian troops could close that.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side B's strength (Bodart 83,000; Victoires more than eighty thousand on 25 November, eighty-two thousand and forty on the 27th, nearly a hundred thousand on the eve of the battle, a hundred thousand in the proclamation; Schönhals nearly 89.000 on the 25th and 82575 in its order of battle); the Austrians (Bodart 16,000; Victoires about eighteen thousand); the Russian guard (Victoires nine thousand and eight thousand five hundred; Schönhals 10.000 men and 6000 horses, and 9380 men and 2900 horses in its table); side A's loss (Bodart 10,000 killed and wounded; Victoires two thousand dead and four or five thousand wounded; Dumas, by Schönhals, 800 dead and 6000 wounded); side B's loss (Bodart 36,000, of which 20,000 prisoners and 6,000 Austrians; Victoires more than forty thousand; Schönhals 5922 Austrians and about 15.000 Russian prisoners and 5000 to 6000 Russian dead and wounded); prisoners, generals, guns and flags (Bodart; Victoires's narrative; the proclamation); the drowning (Victoires against Schönhals); Oudinot's grenadiers (Schönhals p. 169 against p. 167, OCR); Valhubert's death (Victoires p. 267 against p. 271). The accounts agree on the date, the allied flank march against the French right, the French attack on the Pratzen heights, the break of the allied centre, Bagration's attack on the santon, the French holding of the allied position of the day before and the allied retreat to Hodiegitz.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 114 battalions and 83,000 for side B agree with Schönhals's order of battle, his 65,000 for side A with the French figure Schönhals reports and Dumas's, and his 45 flags with Victoires's narrative; his cavalry, squadrons, guns, losses and Austrians are not in the passages read); Victoires et conquêtes, t. XV (the French compilation of 1819; it prints Napoleon's proclamation and puts the French loss as estimated at the time from the corps' reports, and how far its narrative depends on the bulletins was not checked); Schönhals (the Austrian account written in 1831 and printed in 1873, which by its preface draws what it says of the French army's operations from that army's bulletins, and here cites Dumas for the French figures, so for side A the two accounts may share French sources; on side B's strength, losses and the drowning they differ).
